thread.title: Apple iPhone X demand: More data, more questions - MarketWatch

author: Emily Bary
title: Apple iPhone X demand: More data, more questions - MarketWatch
text:
Nearly three months after the iPhone X went on sale, analysts are still debating supply and demand, though the tone has changed.
Initially, the big question was whether Apple Inc. AAPL, -0.88% would be able to produce iPhone X devices quickly enough to meet demand for the phone , which was expected to drive a “supercycle” of upgrades. Now, however, analysts are wondering whether Apple might be easing up on build orders for the phone given that interest hasn’t quite manifested as anticipated, and whether this even matters for the stock.
On Wednesday alone, four analysts revealed their views on rumblings from the Apple supply chain. Another chimed in Thursday. They diverged on many points, including how useful supply-chain data points are, whether demand is indeed weak, and whether Apple shares will be negatively affected in the months to come.

MarketWatch noted in December that analysts observing the same kinds of data points for the holiday quarter also had vastly different viewpoints on how well the iPhone X was actually selling. Now, looking at the March quarter, the team at J.P. Morgan believes that iPhone X contract build orders could fall 50% sequentially, which is a more significant decline than they anticipate for the iPhone 8 and 8 Plus, two less exciting models that Apple debuted in the fall.
“Despite robust revenue from iPhone X suppliers in [the December quarter], demand has gone sour quickly,” wrote Narci Chang, who covers the Asia supply chain for J.P. Morgan. The firm’s European team downgraded shares of sensor supplier AMS AG AMS, -0.03% while U.S. semiconductor analysts trimmed March projections for Qorvo Inc. QRVO, -0.96% among others.
Instinet analyst Jeffrey Kvaal has a similarly negative view of the Apple supply chain , and he argues that it “mirrors [the] demand picture.” Strong December sales for Foxconn Technology Group, formally known as Hon Hai Precision Industry Co. 2317, -0.52% could be a sign of cuts in 2018, he wrote. And on demand, Kvaal is concerned by figures from Verizon Communications Inc.’s VZ, +0.19% recent earnings report , in which the company disclosed an upgrade rate of 7.2% for its December quarter. That rate is below the 9.8% that the firm reported following the iPhone 6 launch, considered to be Apple’s original “supercycle.”
Also troubling to Kvaal: The 7.2% upgrade rate is below the 8.4% and 8.3% that Verizon recorded following the iPhone 6S and 7 launches, respectively. Those refreshes didn’t feature as dramatic changes to the iPhone’s design.
Bernstein’s Toni Sacconaghi joined the chorus, citing “mixed to negative” supply chain indicators and delivering a weak projection for March-quarter iPhone units. Based on his look at suppliers whose revenues tend to correlate highly with iPhone unit numbers, he wrote that December-quarter numbers don’t look risky, but also that “implied iPhone unit guidance for March could be potentially well below consensus estimates.”
Analysts on average project 61 million iPhones will be sold during the March quarter, according to FactSet, but Sacconaghi thinks it’s possible that the company might only report 51 million to 57 million sales. That implies a decline in the upgrade rate, he wrote, “despite initial expectations that this would be a supercycle.”
Whether such data points indicate trouble for Apple’s stock remains a tougher question, he added. While March-quarter iPhone units could disappoint, he noted that plenty of supply-chain indications of this possibility are already out there. Plus, he wrote that the iPhone X’s lofty price tag is expected to deliver a nice boost to average selling prices and, accordingly, revenue.
Meanwhile, Morgan Stanley’s Katy Huberty deemed supply-chain indicators “largely noise.” Though she lowered her price target to $200 from $205 on Thursday and trimmed March-quarter estimates, she still thinks the first three months of 2018 will be strong. Her iPhone-sales projections of 64.5 million are significantly above the 61 million consensus, and her $815 estimate for iPhone average selling price exceeded consensus expectations of $752. She believes that other analysts are underestimating the mix of more expensive iPhones.

At least one analyst is feeling more upbeat about Apple amid the recent data points. Canaccord’s Michael Walkley raised his target price on shares to $200 from $195 on Wednesday, acknowledging that January demand seems “seasonal,” whereas December-quarter demand looked “strong.” Still, he sees the “increased mix of larger screen OLED phones” helping Apple drive strong iPhone sales this year and next.
Apple shares have declined 1.1% over the past month amid the rumblings, though they’re still up 42% in the past 12 months. The Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA, +0.63% , which counts Apple as a component, is up 31% in that time. Analysts and investors will be paying close attention to Apple’s March quarter forecast, expected with the company’s Feb. 1 first-quarter earnings release, for signs of how demand is playing out in 2018 and whether it’s prices or unit sales driving revenues.
